title: What have you been up to?
goals: Catch up with someone: What have you been doing lately? / I've been going to a class since September.
Tell apart the present perfect continuous (activity in progress) from the present perfect (result, quantity).
Express duration with since, for and in, and use already, still and yet clearly.
Talk about films: genres, effects, endings and reviews.
Contrast ideas with although, even though and even if when writing a review.
Ask for a favor politely: I was wondering if you could…

learn.title: Present perfect continuous vs. present perfect
learn.html:
Both tenses connect the past with the present, but they focus on different things.

Present perfect continuousPresent perfect
Formhave / has + been + verb-inghave / has + past participle
Focusan activity in progress or repeated that started earlier and continues until nowa result or quantity: how many things, how many times
ExampleI've been going to a pottery class since September.I've made eight vases so far.
QuestionWhat have you been doing lately? Have you been taking any classes?How many bowls have you made?
  • The continuous is also used for an activity that has just finished and is visible: You're dirty! What have you been doing?
  • State verbs (know, like, have, be, want, believe) are not used in the continuous: I've known her for years.
  • With how long the continuous is preferred for activities: How long have you been studying English?
  • Common words: lately, recently, so far, all day, these days.

watch.why: A situation that started in the past and continues now uses the present perfect (continuous), not the present.

watch.wrong: I've been knowing her for years.
watch.why: Know is a state verb: it is not used in the continuous.

watch.wrong: I've been making eight bowls so far.
watch.right: I've made eight bowls so far.
watch.why: When you talk about results, use the present perfect simple.

watch.wrong: Have you been took any classes?
watch.right: Have you been taking any classes?
watch.why: After been comes a verb with -ing.

learn.title: since, for and in for duration
learn.html:
To say how long something that started earlier and reaches up to today lasts:

WordUsed withExample
sincea point in time (year, month, day, hour, or an action)since September / since 2020 / since I saw you last
fora period of time (amount)for two months / for nine years / for a long time
ina period, only in negatives (equivalent to for)I haven't been out to eat in months. / in ages
  • Since can also be a conjunction: What have you been doing since I saw you last? (after since + past simple).
  • Don't use the present with these expressions: I live here since 2018 is incorrect in English.
  • Lately and recently go with the present perfect; so far usually goes at the end or at the beginning.

watch.wrong: I've been here since three hours.
watch.right: I've been here for three hours.
watch.why: Since needs a point in time; three hours is a period.
2018 is a point in time: since.

watch.wrong: I've worked there from six months.
watch.right: I've worked there for six months.
watch.why: From does not work for duration up to now: use for.

learn.title: already, still and yet with the present perfect
learn.html:
These three words show how an action relates to what you expected.

WordMeaningPositionExample
yetup to now (it is expected to happen); questions and negativesat the endHave you seen it yet? No, I haven't seen it yet. / No, not yet.
alreadyalready (before now)after have or at the endI've already seen it. / I've seen it already.
stillstill (negative: I've been wanting to and it hasn't happened)before haven't / hasn'tI still haven't seen it.
  • I haven't seen it yet is neutral; I still haven't seen it shows impatience or frustration.
  • In American English the past simple is accepted: Did you see it yet? / I already saw it.
  • Don't mix them: Have you already seen it yet? is redundant.

watch.why: In negatives use yet (or still before haven't), not already.
For something that has already happened use already; yet goes at the end in questions and negatives.

learn.title: although, even though, even if: contrasting ideas
learn.html:
To join two ideas that seem not to match (contrast) and write richer reviews:

ConnectorMeaningExample
althoughalthough (real fact, neutral)Although the story seems for children, adults enjoy it, too.
even thoughalthough (real fact, stronger: «despite the fact that»)Even though I don't usually like musicals, I loved this one.
even ifeven if, «it doesn't matter whether» (hypothetical)Even if you don't like musicals, you might enjoy this one.
  • They can go at the beginning (with a comma) or in the middle without a comma: I loved it although it was long.
  • Don't use but in the other part: Although it was long, I loved it. (not Although… , but…).
  • After these connectors comes a complete sentence (subject + verb).
  • Even if almost always goes with the present or a hypothetical past: Even if it rains, we'll go.

watch.wrong: Although it was expensive, but I bought it.
watch.right: Although it was expensive, I bought it.
watch.why: Although already expresses the contrast: it does not take but.

watch.wrong: Even if I was tired yesterday, I went out.
watch.right: Even though I was tired yesterday, I went out.
watch.why: A real past fact calls for even though; even if is for possibilities.

watch.wrong: Although of the rain, we went out.
watch.right: Although it was raining, we went out.
watch.why: Although is followed by subject + verb, not by of.

learn.title: Asking for a favor politely
learn.html:
To ask for an important favor or in formal situations:

  • I was wondering, could you…? — I was wondering, could you write a reference for me?
  • I was wondering if I / you could… — I was wondering if I could ask you something. (after wondering if use could, not can)
  • I wanted to… — Well, I wanted to ask a favor, actually.
  • Would it be all right / OK with you if I + past…? — Would it be OK with you if I picked it up next Monday?

To accept: Sure. / All right. / OK. / No problem.

To move on to another topic or stage of the conversation: All right. So, what can I do for you?

To show that you understand: Right. You need them for your presentation.

write.prompt: Write an email of 180 to 250 words to a friend you haven't seen for a long time. Tell them what you have been doing lately (activities with the present perfect continuous and since/for), what you have achieved so far (present perfect, with so far or already), something you haven't done yet (yet / still), and ask for a favor politely (I was wondering if you could…).
targets: present perfect continuous vs. present perfect
checklist: 180–250 words, with a greeting and a closing
At least 3 sentences with have/has been + -ing
Since for a point in time and for for a period
One sentence with already, one with yet and one with still
Results with the present perfect (so far)
A favor with I was wondering if … could
State verbs without the continuous (know, have)
write.model:
Hi Carla,

How are you? I haven't seen you for ages, and I wanted to tell you what I have been doing lately. I have been working on a big project at my company since January, and I have been studying English for six months. I have also been running every morning, so I feel much healthier.

So far, I have finished my first course and I have saved enough money for a trip. I have already booked the flights to Oaxaca, and I have visited two of the places on my list. My brother has been helping me with the planning, but I still haven't decided which hotel to stay in, and I haven't bought the tickets for the tour yet. I know the city better now, and I have a new apartment, too.

As you live near the bank, I was wondering if you could do me a favor. Would it be possible for you to collect a package for me next week? I'm not sure I'll be home, and I don't want it to be lost. I would be very grateful, and I will invite you to lunch to thank you.

Write to me when you can! I haven't heard your news for a long time, and I'm still waiting for the photos of your holiday.

Hugs,
Mariana

write.prompt: Write a review of 180 to 250 words of a film you have seen. Include the genre, a short plot summary (no spoilers), effects, acting, music and the ending; use review adjectives (stunning, memorable, thrilling…), at least two contrast connectors (although, even though, even if) and end with a recommendation.
checklist: 180–250 words
The genre and theme of the film
At least 3 review adjectives
At least 2 contrast connectors (no but next to although)
One sentence with even if
No spoilers about the ending
A final recommendation (I highly recommend…)
write.model:
The Last Lighthouse is a thrilling adventure drama that tells the story of a young engineer who is sent to repair an old lighthouse on a remote island. The main theme is loneliness and the fear of the unknown, and the director builds the tension slowly and carefully.

The plot is simple, but it keeps you interested from the first minute. Although the story takes place in only one location, the film never feels boring. The special effects are stunning, especially during the storm scenes, when the waves seem to come out of the screen. The acting is also very good. The lead actress gives a memorable performance, and even though she speaks very little, her face says everything. The music is another strong point. The soundtrack is quiet and mysterious, and it makes the most important scenes more emotional.

Of course, the film is not perfect. The first half is a bit slow, and some characters are not developed enough. Even if you usually prefer action movies, I think you will enjoy the atmosphere. I will not say anything about the ending, but it is surprising, and it made me think for days.

Overall, it is a beautiful and intelligent film. I highly recommend it to anyone who likes mystery and wants to see something different at the cinema.

reading.title: An email to an old friend
reading.intro: Read Valeria's email to her friend Sofía and answer.
paragraphs: Hi Sofia, I can't believe it's been almost a year since we last talked! What have you been doing lately? Please write soon. I want to hear everything. I've been so busy since I started my new job in Querétaro, but I'm finally taking a day off tomorrow, so I have time to write you a long message.

Let me catch up with you first. I've been living here for eight months now, and I've been going to a pottery class since September. I've already made six bowls and two vases, although they're not very beautiful yet. My teacher says I still haven't learned to center the clay, but I haven't given up. I've also been taking a weight training class on Saturdays. Honestly, I haven't felt this strong in ages, and I've been sleeping much better, too. My coworkers say I look happier, and I think they're right. Living in a new city has been difficult, but these small activities have helped me meet interesting people.

Last weekend I finally saw The Last Lighthouse, the movie everybody has been talking about. You know I don't usually like fantasy films, but I loved this one. Even though it's almost three hours long, I never looked at my watch. The special effects are stunning, the costumes are magnificent, and the music is mesmerizing. The story takes place on a small island, where a young woman discovers a secret in an old lighthouse. I won't spoil it for you, but there's a sad ending, and I cried for ten minutes. It's a real tearjerker!

My brother hasn't seen it yet, but he's already planning to go this Friday. He says he'll watch it even if the reviews are bad. Typical! He has been working at a theater downtown since last year, so he sees a lot of movies for free. He tells me the sequel will come out in November, and the director has promised an even bigger story. I'm not sure the second film can be better than the first, but I'm curious. Since I moved here, I haven't had much time for the theater, so this weekend was a real treat. I went alone, bought a huge bag of popcorn, and enjoyed every minute without checking my phone once.

Have you seen it yet? If not, I was wondering if you could come to Querétaro next month. We could go to the theater together and then have dinner. I'd also like to ask you a favor: could you send me the recipe for your grandmother's mole? I've been trying to make it for weeks, and it never tastes right. I still haven't found the secret! Write soon, and tell me everything. Hugs, Valeria
